Surat al-Nasr

It has three verses and is Medinan.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿When the help of God comes﴾.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿When the help of God comes﴾. There are subtle points in this verse:

The first: When God Most High promised Muhammad a great upbringing, saying, ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 4], and His saying, ﴿Indeed, We have granted you al-Kawthar﴾ [al-Kawthar: 1], his affairs necessarily increased every day. It is as if God Most High said: "O Muhammad, why is your heart constricted? Did I not, when you were not yet commissioned, not abandon you, but help you with the birds in flocks? At the beginning of your mission I increased this, making the birds into angels: ﴿Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforces you with three thousand angels﴾ [Al 'Imran: 124]. Now I will increase further and say: I Myself will be your helper: ﴿When the help of God comes﴾."

Then he said: "My God, the blessing is only complete when You open for me the house of my birth and my dwelling." He said, "And the conquest" [i.e., the answer was given by the phrase "and the conquest"]. He said: "My God, but when the people leave, what pleasure is there in that?" He said: ﴿And you see people entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾. Then it is as if He said: "Do you know, O Muhammad, for what reason you were given these three honours? You were given them because you said in the previous surah: ﴿Say: O disbelievers! I do not worship what you worship﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1–2]. This contains three matters:

First: You helped Me with your tongue, so its recompense was: ﴿When the help of God comes﴾.

Second: Mecca opened your heart to the army of monotheism, so We gave you the conquest of Mecca, which is what is meant by His saying, ﴿and the conquest﴾.

Third: You brought the subjects of your limbs and members into obedience and servitude to Me, so I too brought My servants into obedience to you. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿entering the religion of God in multitudes﴾. Then, after you received these three robes of honour, send to My presence three kinds of servitude: ‘Give gifts to one another, and you will love one another.’ If I help you, then glorify; if you conquer Mecca, then praise; if they embrace Islam, then seek forgiveness. He placed glorification in response to ﴿the help of God﴾, because glorification is the declaration of God's transcendence above resemblance to created things; that is, you witness that He has helped you. So beware lest you think that He helped you because you deserved that help from Him. Rather, believe in His being exalted above anyone among creation having a claim upon Him for anything. Then He placed praise in response to the conquest of Mecca, because a blessing can only be answered with praise. Then He placed seeking forgiveness in response to people entering the religion, which is what is meant by His saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad: 19]. That is, the multitude of followers is something that occupies the heart with the pleasure of status and acceptance, so seek forgiveness for this measure of your sin. And seek forgiveness for their sins, for the more they are, the more their sins are, and so their need for your seeking forgiveness is greater.

The second aspect: When he, peace be upon him, disavowed disbelief and confronted them with harshness in His saying, ﴿Say: O disbelievers!﴾ [al-Kafirun: 1], it is as if he feared some of the people, so he lessened that severity, and said: ﴿To you is your religion, and to me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6]. It was said: "O Muhammad, do not fear. I will not take you to the help; rather, I will bring the help to you: ﴿When the help of God comes﴾." Its parallel is: "The earth was folded up for me" [a hadith], meaning: do not go to the earth; rather the earth will come to you. If you tire of staying and wish to journey, then someone like you does not travel except to within two bow-lengths: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night﴾ [al-Isra': 1]. Moreover, I will add to this, and favour the poor among your community over their rich, then command the rich to sacrifice animals so that they may take them as mounts. If a poor man remains without a mount, I will drive Paradise to him: ﴿And Paradise is brought near for the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 90].

The third aspect: It is as if He, glorified be He, said: "O Muhammad, the world's turbidity is never pure, its trials never last, nor its blessings. You rejoiced in al-Kawthar, so bear the hardship of the foolishness of fools, when they said: 'Worship our gods until we worship your God.' When he disavowed them and his heart was constricted because of them, He said: 'Rejoice, for the help of God has come.' When he rejoiced, He said: 'Depart, depart! Do you not know that after perfection there must be decline? So seek His forgiveness. O human, do not grieve over the hunger of spring, for after it comes the richness of autumn; and do not rejoice in the richness of autumn, for after it comes the loneliness of winter. Thus, whoever has his fortune complete will have nothing left but change." And from this is the saying:

"When a matter is complete, its decline draws near;
expect a fall when it is said, 'It is complete.'"

My God, why did You do this?

He said: "So that We do not let your heart rest upon the world, but that you may always be on the wing of departure and travel."

The fourth aspect: When He said at the end of the previous surah, ﴿To you is your religion, and to me is my religion﴾ [al-Kafirun: 6], it is as if he said: "My God, what is my reward?" He said: "The help of God." He said: "And what is the recompense of my uncle, when he called me to worship idols?" He said: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [al-Masad: 1]. If it is asked: "Why did He begin with the promise before the threat?" We say: for several reasons:

One: because His mercy precedes His wrath.

The second: so that the category is connected to the category, for He said ﴿to me is my religion﴾, and that is the help, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day when some faces will be white and some faces will be black; as for those whose faces are black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106].

The third: fulfilling a promise is more important in generosity than fulfilling a threat of retribution. Reflect on these correspondences between these surahs, although this surah is among the last revealed in Medina and that surah is among the first revealed in Mecca, so that it may be known that the arrangement of these surahs is from God and by His command.

The fifth aspect: In the previous surah He did not mention any of God's names; rather He said, "what I worship," using the word "what," as if He said: "I will not mention the name of God, lest they take it lightly and their punishment increases." In this surah He mentioned His greatest name, because it is sent down to the beloved ones, so that their reward for reciting it may be greater. It is as if He, glorified be He, said: "Do not mention My name in the presence of the disbelievers, lest they disgrace it; and mention it with the allies, so that they may honour it."

The sixth aspect: The grammarians said: "‘Idha' (when) is in the accusative, governed by ‘sabbih' (glorify)," and the implied meaning is: "So glorify your Lord with praise when the help of God comes." It is as if He, glorified be He, says: "I have made the time a vessel for what you desire, which is help, conquest, and victory, and I have filled that vessel with these things, and I have sent it to you. So do not return it to Me empty; rather fill it with servitude, so that the meaning of ‘give gifts to one another, and you will love one another’ may be realised." It is as if Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: "With what shall I fill the vessel of your gift, when I am poor?" God says, in meaning: "If you find nothing else, then at least move your tongue with glorification, praise, and seeking forgiveness." So when Muhammad, prayers and peace be upon him, did that, the meaning of "give gifts to one another" was achieved, and therefore love was achieved. For this reason Muhammad is the beloved of God.

[Page 140]

The seventh aspect: It is as if God, Most High, says: "When victory, conquest, and the entry of people into your religion come to you, occupy yourself also with glorification, praise, and seeking forgiveness, for I have said: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ [Ibrahim: 7]. Your occupation with these acts of obedience will be a cause for increasing your ranks in this world and the Hereafter, and you will continue to ascend, until the promise becomes, by My saying: ‘We have granted you al-Kawthar.'"

The eighth aspect: Faith is only complete through two matters: negation and affirmation, and disavowal and allegiance. Negation and disavowal are His saying, ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾, and affirmation and allegiance are His saying, ﴿When the help of God comes﴾. These are the general aspects related to this surah.

Know that there are secrets in the verse, and their explanation can only be presented in the form of question and answer.

First question: What is the difference between help and conquest, such that conquest is conjoined to help?

The answer has several aspects:

One: Help is assistance in attaining the sought-after goal, and conquest is the attainment of the goal that was sought. It is clear that help is like the cause of conquest, so for this reason it begins with mentioning help and conjoins conquest to it.

Two: It may be said: help is the perfection of religion, and conquest is worldly prosperity, which is the completion of blessing. A parallel to this verse is His saying: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My blessing upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3].

Three: Help is victory in this world over one's desires, and conquest is by Paradise, as He said: ﴿And its gates will be opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. The most evident opinion regarding help is that it is domination over Quraysh, or over all the Arabs.

Second question: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was always victorious through proofs and miracles, so what is the meaning of restricting the word "help" to the conquest of Mecca?

The answer has two aspects:

One of them: The help meant here is the help that agrees with natural inclination. The unrestricted word "help" was made to indicate this particular help, because this help, due to its great place in the hearts of the people of this world, made what preceded it like nonexistence, just as the one rewarded upon entering Paradise is imagined as if he had never tasted any blessing at all. The reference to this meaning is in His saying: ﴿And they were shaken until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214].

The other: Perhaps what is meant is the help of God in worldly matters, which He decreed for His prophets, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the term of God, when it comes, will not be delayed﴾ [Nuh: 4].

Third question: Help comes only from God, as He, Most High, said: ﴿And there is no help except from God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 126]. So what is the benefit of this restriction, namely His saying, ﴿the help of God﴾?

The answer: its meaning is a help that befits none but God, and none should do it except God, or that it is befitting only to His wisdom. It is said, "This is the craftsmanship of Zayd," when Zayd is well known for perfecting craftsmanship, and what is meant is to magnify the state of that craftsmanship. So it is here as well. Or [it means] the help of God because it is a response to their supplication: ﴿When is the help of God?﴾, so He says, "This is what you asked for."

Fourth question: Describing help as "coming" is a metaphor; its literal form would be "when the help of God occurs." So what is the benefit of abandoning the literal expression and mentioning the metaphor?

The answer contains several indications:

One: Affairs are tied to their times, and God has ordained specific causes for the occurrence of each event and fixed times in which advance, delay, change, and alteration are impossible. When that time arrives and that moment comes, that effect comes with it. To this refers His saying: ﴿And there is nothing but that with Us are its treasures, and We do not send it down except in a known measure﴾ [al-Hijr: 21].

Two: The wording indicates that help was as though longing for Muhammad (ﷺ). This is because that help was deserved by him by the rule of the promise, so the requirement was present, but the non-occurrence of the effect was due to the absence of a condition. It is like a heavy object suspended: its weight necessitates falling, but the hanging cord prevents it. The heavy object is then like one longing to fall. So too here, help was like one longing for Muhammad (ﷺ).

Three: The realm of non-existence is a realm without end, the realm of darkness, but at its depths is a spring of generosity and mercy, which is the spring of God's generosity and His bringing into being. Then the seas of generosity and lights branched out and began to flow, and their flowing necessitates their arriving at a specific place and location at every moment. So the seas of God's mercy and His help have been flowing from eternity. It is as if it was said: "O Muhammad, their arrival to you is near. So when the waves of this sea come to you, occupy yourself with glorification, praise, and seeking forgiveness, for these three are the ship without which escape from the seas of lordship is impossible." For this reason, when your father Noah rode the sea of wrath and pride, he sought help by saying: ﴿In the name of God is its course and its anchorage﴾ [Hud: 41].

**The fifth question:** There is no doubt that those who helped the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to conquer Mecca were the Companions, from the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the Helpers (al-Ansar). Then He called their support for the Messenger of God "the help of God" (﴿nașr Allah﴾). What is the reason that the act proceeding from them is attributed to God?

**The answer:** This is a sea from which the sea of the secret of divine decree and predestination (al-qada' wa-l-qadar) flows. Their act is God's act. The explanation is that their actions are ascribed to what is in their hearts of motives (dawa'i) and deterrents (sawarif). These motives and deterrents are originated things (umur hadithah), so they must have an originator, and it is not the servant, for otherwise an infinite regress (tasalsul) would follow. Therefore it must be God, the Exalted. So the first principle and the most remote efficient cause is God, the Exalted, and the nearest principle is the servant. From this perspective, the help attributed to the Companions is itself attributed to God, the Exalted.

If it is said: On this assumption that you have stated, the act of the servant would be a consequence of the act of God, the Exalted, and this contradicts the text, for He said: ﴿If you help God, He will help you﴾ (Muhammad 7), thus making our help to Him precede His help to us.

The answer: There is no impossibility that an act proceeds from the Real (al-Haqq), and that this becomes a cause for an act proceeding from us. Then our act leads on to another act that proceeds from the Lord. The causes of events and their effects form a chain in an amazing order, the manner of which most human minds are unable to grasp.

**The sixth question:** The word "idha" (when) is for the future. Here, when He mentioned a future promise of victory, He said: ﴿When the help of God comes﴾, and He named Himself by the Name "God". But when He mentioned past help, He said: ﴿If help comes from your Lord, they will surely say﴾ (al-Ankabut 10), and named Him with the word "Lord". What is the reason for this?

**The answer:** Because He, the Exalted, after the act has occurred, becomes "Lord" (rabb). Before it, He was not "Lord" in that sense, though He was "God" (ilah).

**The seventh question:** He, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you help God, He will help you﴾. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, helped God when he said: ﴿Say: O disbelievers, I do not worship what you worship﴾ (al-Kafirun 1–2). So by the judgment of this promise it was obligatory for God to help him. Hence He said: ﴿When the help of God comes﴾. Do you say that this help was obligatory upon Him?

**The answer:** What is not obligatory may become obligatory by a promise. That is why it is said: "The promise of the generous is more binding than the debt of the creditor." Moreover, it is obligatory for a father to help his son and for a master to help his slave. Indeed, help becomes obligatory even upon a stranger when it is specifically required of him, if he is the only one (able to help), by consensus, even if he is busy with his own prayer. All these grounds are combined in His, the Exalted, case. So He promised, with generosity, and He is more compassionate to His servant than a father to his son or a master to his slave. He is Protector (wali) by way of ownership and Master (mawla) by way of sovereignty, and Sustainer (qayyum) for management, and the One, the Unique, having no second. Therefore it became incumbent upon Him, by the obligation of generosity, to help His servant. For this reason He said: ﴿When the help of God comes﴾.

As for His saying, the Exalted, "and the conquest" (wa-l-fath), there are several issues:

**The first issue:** It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the conquest is the conquest of Mecca, which is the conquest that is called "the conquest of conquests" (fath al-futuh). It is narrated that when the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah took place and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) departed, some of those who were in the covenant of Quraysh raided Khuza'ah, and they were in the covenant of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The envoy of that people came and informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and that was grave for him. Then he said: "Indeed, this (raid) informs me that victory comes from God." Then he said to his Companions: "Look, Abu Sufyan will come and seek to renew the covenant." Before an hour had passed, the man came seeking that, but the Messenger did not answer him, nor did the chief Companions. So he took refuge with Fatimah, but that did not benefit him, and he returned to Mecca in despair. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) prepared to march to Mecca.

Then it is narrated that Sarrah, a freedwoman of some of the Banu Hashim, came to Medina. He, peace be upon him, said to her: "Have you come as a Muslim?" She said: "No, but you were the masters (al-mawali), and I am in need." So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) urged the Banu 'Abd al-Muttalib, and they clothed her, carried her, and provided for her. Then Hatib came to her with ten dinars and asked her to carry a letter to Mecca, its text being: "Know that the Messenger of God is coming to you, so take your precaution." Sarrah set out, and Gabriel descended with the news. So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent 'Ali, peace be upon him, and 'Ammar with a group, and ordered them to take the letter, or else strike off her neck. When they caught up with her, she denied it and swore. 'Ali, peace be upon him, drew his sword and said: "By God, we have not been lied to." So she brought it out from the braid of her hair. The Prophet summoned Hatib and said: "What led you to do this?" He said: "By God, I have not disbelieved since I embraced Islam, nor have I loved them since I parted from them. But I was a stranger among Quraysh, and all those with you from the Emigrants have relatives in Mecca who protect their families. I feared for my family, so I wanted to make a hand (favor) with them." 'Umar said: "Let me strike the neck of this hypocrite." He said: "And what do you know, O 'Umar? Perhaps God has looked upon the people of Badr and said: 'Do as you wish, for I have forgiven you.'" 'Umar's eyes then overflowed. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) set out until he halted at Marr al-Zahran. Al-'Abbas and Abu Sufyan came to him and asked permission, and he granted permission to his uncle only. Abu Sufyan said: "Either you permit me, or I shall take my son into the desert, where he will die of hunger and thirst." His heart softened, so he permitted him and said to him: "Has the time not come for you to submit and to affirm the Oneness?" He said: "I think that He is One, and if there were another god besides God, He would have helped us." He said: "Has the time not come for you to know that I am His Messenger?" He said: "I still have doubt about that." Al-'Abbas said: "Submit before 'Umar kills you." He said: "And what shall I do about al-'Uzza?" 'Umar said: "Were it not that you are in the presence of the Messenger of God, I would strike your neck." He said: "O Muhammad, is it not better for you to leave these riffraff, and to reconcile with your people and your kinsmen? The inhabitants of Mecca are your kin and relatives, so do not expose them to raiding and attack." He, peace be upon him, said: "These are the ones who helped me and assisted me and defended my sanctuary. And the people of Mecca expelled me and wronged me. If they are captured, it is because of their evil deeds." He ordered al-'Abbas to take him and station him at the lookout post so that he might observe the army. The troops passed by him, and he would ask: "Who is this?" Al-'Abbas would say: "This is so-and-so, one of the commanders of the army," until the green battalion came, of which only the eyes could be seen. He asked about them, and al-'Abbas said: "This is the Messenger of God." He said: "Your nephew has been given a great kingdom." Al-'Abbas said: "It is prophethood." He said: "Far from it, prophethood!" Then he advanced and entered Mecca, and said: "Muhammad has come with an army that no one can withstand." Hind shouted and said: "Kill this announcer," and seized his beard. The man cried out and pushed her away from himself. When Abu Sufyan heard the people's call to the dawn prayer, and they were ten thousand, he was greatly alarmed and asked al-'Abbas, who informed him about the prayer. The Messenger of God entered Mecca on his riding beast, with his beard upon the pommel of his saddle, bowed as if prostrating, in humility and gratitude. Then Abu Sufyan asked for safe-conduct, and he said: "Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe." He said: "And who can the house of mine contain?" He said: "Whoever enters the mosque is safe." He said: "And who can the mosque contain?" He said: "Whoever lays down his weapons is safe, and whoever closes his door is safe." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) stood at the door of the mosque and said: "There is no god but God alone; He fulfilled His promise, helped His servant, and defeated the confederates alone." Then he said: "O people of Mecca, what do you think I will do with you?" They said: "Good. You are a noble brother and the son of a noble brother." He said: "Go, for you are the freed ones (al-Tulaqa')." So he freed them. For this reason the people of Mecca were called "the freed ones." From this, 'Ali, peace be upon him, used to say to Mu'awiyah: "How can the client (mawla) and the freed slave (al-mu'takt) be equal?" He meant: "We freed you when God empowered us over your necks." But he did not say: "Go, for you are freed (mu'taqun)," rather he said "al-Tulaqa'," because a freed slave may be returned to slavery, whereas a divorced woman (al-mutallaqah) may be returned to the bondage of marriage. They were still upon disbelief, so it was permissible that they might betray, and their servitude could be lawfully taken again. Also, divorce pertains to women, and they had laid down their arms and taken dwellings, like women. Also, the freed slave is released and goes wherever he wishes, whereas the divorced woman sits in the house for the waiting period ('iddah), and they were ordered to remain in Mecca like women.

Then the people pledged allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) upon Islam, and they began to enter the religion of God in multitudes. It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, prayed eight rak'ahs: four for the forenoon prayer (salat al-duha), and four more as thanks to God, as a supererogatory prayer. This is the story of the conquest of Mecca.

The well-known view among the exegetes is that the intended meaning of "the conquest" in this surah is the conquest of Mecca. Among the indications that the intended meaning of "the conquest" is the conquest of Mecca is that He, the Exalted, mentioned it linked with "the help." Help may occur without conquest, as at Badr, and conquest may occur without help, as the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, for He conquered the town but did not take the people. But on the day of the conquest of Mecca, both help and conquest came together, and the creation became as slaves to Him until He freed them.

**The second view:** The intended meaning is the conquest of Khaybar, which was at the hand of 'Ali, peace be upon him, and the story is well known. It is narrated that he took along Khalid ibn al-Walid, who used to vie with him in courage. When the ladder was set up, he said to Khalid: "Will you go first?" He said: "No." When 'Ali, peace be upon him, went first, he asked him: "How many (steps) did you climb?" He said: "I do not know, from the intensity of fear." It is also narrated that he said to 'Ali, peace be upon him: "Will you not wrestle with me?" He said: "Did I not throw you down?" He said: "Yes, but that was before my Islam." Perhaps 'Ali, peace be upon him, refrained from wrestling with him so that his reputation in Islam would be that he was a man from whom 'Ali refrains. Or 'Ali would say: "I threw you down when you were a disbeliever; now that you are a Muslim, it is not fitting that I throw you down."

**The third view:** He conquered al-Ta'if, and its story is long.

**The fourth view:** The intended meaning is the victory over the disbelievers and the conquest of the lands of polytheism in general. This is the view of Abu Muslim.

**The fifth view:** By "the conquest" is meant what God opened to him of knowledge. From this is His saying: ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ (Ta-Ha 114). But the attainment of knowledge must be preceded by the expansion of the breast and the purity of the heart, and that is what is meant by His saying: ﴿When the help of God comes﴾. It is possible that the intended meaning of "the help of God" is His assisting him in obedience and good deeds, and "the conquest" is the opening of the world of intelligibles and spiritual realities.

**The second issue:** If we take "the conquest" to mean the conquest of Mecca, then there are two views among people concerning the time of the revelation of this surah:

One of them: The conquest of Mecca took place in the year 8 AH, and this surah was revealed in the year 10 AH. It is narrated that he lived seventy days after the revelation of this surah, and for this reason it is called "the Surah of Farewell" (surat al-tawdi').

The second view: This surah was revealed before the conquest of Mecca, and it is a promise to the Messenger of God that He would help him against the people of Mecca and grant him its conquest. A parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, He who imposed the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to a place of return﴾ (al-Qasas 85). His saying: ﴿When the help of God and the conquest come﴾ requires the future tense, since one does not say of what has already occurred "when it comes" or "when it occurs." If this view is correct, then this verse is among the miracles, since it is a report whose reported matter came to pass after a time, corresponding to it, and reporting the unseen is a miracle.

**If it is said:** Why was the help mentioned as attributed to God, the Exalted, while the conquest was mentioned with the definite article (al-)?

**The answer:** The definite article is for a previously known referent, so it refers to the conquest of Mecca.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 110, Verse 2:**

[Page 145]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And you see the people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes.﴾ Concerning it there are several issues:

**The first issue:** *ra'ayta* (رَأيْتَ) may mean "you saw" (abṣarta) or "you knew" (ʿalimta). If it means "you saw," then *yadkhulūna* (يَدْخُلُونَ) is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the sense is: "And you saw the people while entering the religion of Allah in multitudes." If it means "you knew," then *yadkhulūna fī dīn Allāh* is the second object of *ʿalimta*, and the sense is: "You knew the people to be entering the religion of Allah."

**The second issue:** The apparent meaning of the word *al-nās* ("the people") is generality. This requires that all people had entered existence, yet the matter was not so. The answer is in two parts:

*The first:* What is intended by humanity and reason is only religion and obedience, as He said: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except to worship Me﴾ [Qur'an 51:56]. Whoever turns away from the true religion and remains in disbelief is, as it were, not a human being. This is the meaning intended by His saying: ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ [Qur'an 7:179], and His saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe"﴾ [Qur'an 2:13]. It was asked of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī (peace be upon him): "Who are the people?" He said: "We are the people, our adherents are the likeness of the people, and our enemies are the *nāsnās* (a worthless, deficient kind)." ʿAlī (peace be upon him) then kissed him between his eyes and said: "Allah knows best where He places His message."

If it is said: they entered Islam only after a long period and with much shortcoming, so how did they deserve this great praise? We say: this indicates the vastness of Allah's mercy. For the servant, after he has committed disbelief and disobedience throughout his life, if he comes to faith at the end of his life, his faith is accepted and he is praised with this great praise. It is related that the angels say to such a person: "You have come, though you had refused." It is also related that he (peace be upon him) said: "Allah is more joyful at the repentance of one of you than a lost person who finds [what he lost], and a thirsty person who reaches water." The meaning is that the Lord, exalted is He, says: "I nurtured him for seventy years; if he dies in his disbelief, I must send him to the Fire, and then My kindness toward him over seventy years is wasted." Thus, the longer the period of disbelief and disobedience, the more strongly the repentance from it is accepted.

*The second answer:* It is related that what is meant by "the people" are the people of Yemen. Abū Hurayrah said: When this sūrah was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah is greatest; the help of Allah and the conquest have come, and the people of Yemen have come. They are a people whose hearts are tender; faith is Yemeni, understanding is Yemeni, and wisdom is Yemeni." And he said: "I find the breath of your Lord coming from the direction of Yemen."

**The third issue:** The majority of jurists and many of the theologians (*mutakallimūn*) said: the faith of the *muqallid* (one who follows by imitation, *taqlīd*) is valid. They argued with this verse, saying: He, exalted is He, judged the faith of those multitudes to be valid and made it one of the greatest favours upon Muḥammad (peace be upon him). Had their faith not been valid, He would not have mentioned it in this context. Furthermore, we know with certainty that they did not know by proof the createdness of bodies (*ḥudūth al-ajsād*), nor the establishment that He, exalted is He, is transcendent above corporeality, place, and direction, nor the establishment that He, exalted is He, knows all knowables, which have no end, nor the establishment of the existence of the complete miracle (*muʿjiz*) through the hand of Muḥammad (ﷺ), nor the establishment of how the existence of the miracle indicates truthfulness. And the knowledge that those Bedouins did not know these subtleties is necessary (*ḍarūrī*). So we know that the faith of the *muqallid* is valid.

It cannot be said that they knew the foundations of the proofs of these issues, because the foundations of these proofs are evident; rather, they were ignorant only of the details. Yet it is not a condition for a person to be a reasoner (*mustadill*) that he know these details. For we say: the proof does not accept increase or decrease. If a proof is, for example, composed of ten premises, and someone knows nine of them but is a *muqallid* regarding the tenth premise, he is necessarily a *muqallid* in the conclusion, because a branch of imitation is more deserving of being imitation. And if he knows the entirety of those ten premises, it is impossible that anyone else be more knowledgeable than him in that proof. For if that extra element is a necessary part of the proof's indication, then the first ten premises were not the complete proof, since with them there must be this additional premise; yet we had supposed those ten to be sufficient. And if the extra element is not necessary for the proof's indication, then it is something separate from that proof and not required for it to be a proof of that conclusion. Thus it is established that knowing that a proof is a proof does not accept increase or decrease.

As for saying that those Bedouins knew all the premises of the proofs of these issues, such that not one of those premises escaped them, that is either obstinacy, or they were not like that. In that case, it is established that they were *muqallidūn*. Among what confirms what we have mentioned is what is related from al-Ḥasan: when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) conquered Mecca, the Arabs turned to one another and said: "If he has prevailed over the people of the Sanctuary, it must be that he is upon the truth, for Allah had protected them from the companions of the Elephant and from everyone who intended them harm." Then they began to enter Islam in multitudes without fighting. This is what al-Ḥasan transmitted. And it is known that reasoning from the fact that he prevailed over the people of Mecca, so it must be that he is upon the truth, is not a sound argument. Thus we know that they were not reasoners but *muqallidūn*.

**The fourth issue:** The religion of Allah is Islam, due to His saying: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Qur'an 3:19], and His saying: ﴿And whoever desires other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Qur'an 3:85]. The religion has other names, among them *al-īmān* (faith). Allah said: ﴿So We brought out whoever was in it of the believers. But We did not find there except one house of the submitting (*muslimīn*)﴾ [Qur'an 51:35–36]. Among them is *al-ṣirāṭ* (the path), as He said: ﴿The path of Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Qur'an 42:53]. Among them is "the word of Allah," and among them is the light: ﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾ [Qur'an 61:8]. Among them is guidance, due to His saying: ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ [Qur'an 16:93]. Among them is the firm handhold: ﴿So he has grasped the most reliable handhold﴾ [Qur'an 31:22]. Among them is the rope: ﴿And hold firmly to the rope of Allah﴾ [Qur'an 3:103]. Among them are *ṣibghat Allāh* (the dye of Allah) and *fiṭrat Allāh* (the natural disposition created by Allah). He said ﴿in the religion of Allah﴾ and did not say "in the religion of the Lord," nor any of the other names, for two reasons:

*The first:* This name is the greatest of names, because it indicates the Essence and the Attributes. It is as if He is saying: this religion, even if it had no quality besides being the religion of Allah, it would be obligatory to accept it.

*The second:* If He had said "the religion of the Lord," that would indicate that this religion is obligatory for you to accept only because He nurtured you and did good to you. Then your obedience to Him would be motivated by seeking benefit, and sincerity would not be attained. So it is as if He is saying: devote your service purely because I am God, not for a benefit that returns to you.

**The fifth issue:** *Al-fawj* (the multitude) is a large group. An entire tribe would enter it, after they had been entering it one by one and two by two. It is related from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh that he wept one day, and it was said to him: "What makes you weep?" He said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'The people entered the religion of Allah in multitudes, and they will leave it in multitudes. We seek refuge in Allah from loss after bounty.'"

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 110, verse 3 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise and seek His forgiveness. Indeed, He is ever Accepting of repentance.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: He, may He be exalted, commanded him to glorify (tasbih), then to praise (hamd), then to seek forgiveness (istighfar). This order has several benefits:

The first benefit: Know that the delay of victory for years, although Muhammad was upon the truth, is something that weighs heavily on the heart, and there arises in the heart the thought: "If I am upon the truth, why do You not help me? And why did You give these disbelievers power over me?" So, to answer this thought, he was commanded to glorify (tasbih). As for according to our view, the purpose of this glorification is that You are exalted above anyone having any claim upon You; rather, everything You do, You do by the judgment of the divine will, so You may do what You wish as You wish. Thus the benefit of glorification is to declare God exalted above anyone having a claim upon Him. As for the view of the Mu'tazilah: the benefit of declaring Him exalted is that the servant knows that that delay was due to wisdom and benefit, not due to stinginess or preferring falsehood over truth. Then, when the servant is free from declaring God exalted above what is not fitting, then he occupies himself with praising Him for the goodness and kindness He has bestowed. Then at that point he occupies himself with seeking forgiveness for the sins of his own self.

The second aspect: The travellers (al-sa'irin) have two paths. Some of them say: "I have not seen anything except that I have seen God after it," and some say: "I have not seen anything except that I have seen God before it." There is no doubt that this path is more perfect. As for according to the sciences of wisdom (al-ma'alim al-hikmiyyah), it is because descending from the influencer (al-mu'aththir) to the effect (al-athar) is of greater rank than ascending from the effect to the influencer. As for according to the thoughts of the masters of spiritual exercises (arbab al-riyadat), it is because the fountain of light is the Necessarily Existent (wajib al-wujud), and the fountain of darkness is the contingently existent (mumkin al-wujud), so immersion in the first is undoubtedly more noble. And because deducing the root from the branch is stronger than deducing the branch from the root. Having established this, we say: The verse indicates this path, which is the more noble of the two paths, because He placed occupation with the Creator before occupation with the self. So He first mentioned two matters concerning the Creator:
One of them: glorification (tasbih).
The second: praise (tahmid). Then they mentioned in the third rank seeking forgiveness, which is a state mixed from attention to the Creator and attention to the creation.

Know that the attributes of the Truth are confined to negation and affirmation, and negations precede affirmations. So glorification is an allusion to addressing the negative attributes that belong to the Necessarily Existent, and these are the attributes of majesty (sifat al-jalal). And praise is an allusion to the affirmative attributes belonging to Him, and these are the attributes of beauty (sifat al-ikram). For this reason the Qur'an indicates the precedence of majesty over beauty. When he alluded to these two kinds through knowledge of the Necessarily Existent, he descended from it to seeking forgiveness, because seeking forgiveness contains the seeing of the deficiency of the self, contains the seeing of the bounty of the Truth, and contains a seeking of what is most fitting and most perfect for the self. It is known that to the degree that the servant is occupied with contemplating other than God, he remains deprived of contemplating the presence of God's majesty. For this subtle reason, He delayed the mention of seeking forgiveness after glorification and praise.

The third aspect: It is a guidance for humanity to resemble the angelic state, because the highest of every kind is joined to the lowest of the higher kind. For this reason it has been said: the last of the levels of humanity is the first of the levels of angelhood. Then the angels said about themselves: ﴿And we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. So His saying here: ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise﴾ is an allusion to resembling the angels in their saying: ﴿And we glorify You with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. And His saying here: (and seek His forgiveness) is an allusion to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and sanctify You﴾, because they explained His saying ﴿and sanctify You﴾ as meaning: we make ourselves holy for the sake of Your pleasure, and seeking forgiveness returns in its meaning also to sanctifying the self. It is also possible that the meaning is that they claimed for themselves that they glorified Me with My praise and saw that from themselves. As for you, so glorify Me with My praise, and seek forgiveness from seeing that obedience from yourself; rather, you must see it as from My grace and kindness. It is also possible to say: the angels, as they said concerning themselves:

﴿And we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾, God said concerning them: ﴿and they seek forgiveness for those who believe﴾ [Ghafir: 7]. So you, O Muhammad, seek forgiveness for those who came in groups, like the angels who seek forgiveness for those who believe and say: "Our Lord, ﴿forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾" [Ghafir: 7].

The fourth aspect: Tasbih is purification (al-tathir). So it is possible that the meaning is: purify the Ka'bah from the idols and break them. Then, when you have done that, it is not fitting that you see yourself as having brought the obedience befitting Him; rather, you must see yourself in this state as falling short, so seek forgiveness for your shortcoming in His obedience.

The fifth aspect: It is as if He, may He be exalted, is saying: O Muhammad, either you are infallible (ma'sum) or you are not infallible. If you are infallible, then occupy yourself with glorification and praise; and if you are not infallible, then occupy yourself with seeking forgiveness. So the verse is like an admonition that there is no freedom from obligation in servitude, as He said: ﴿And worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty﴾ [al-Hijr: 99].

The second issue: Regarding the meaning of tasbih there are two views:
The first: He mentioned God with transcendence (al-tanazzuh). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was asked about it and said: "Declaring God free from every evil." Its origin is from sabaha, for the swimmer swims in water like a bird in air, and controls himself from sinking into it and perishing, or becoming soiled from the place of the water and its course. The intensive form (tashdid) is for distancing, because you "sabbahahu," that is, you distance Him from what is not permissible for Him. The use of it in declaring God free from what is not permissible for Him, of essential and active attributes, negatively and positively, is fitting because just as the fish does not accept impurity, so also the Truth, glory be to Him, does not accept anything unfitting at all. Thus the word indicates transcendence in the essence, the attributes and the acts.
The second view: The meaning of tasbih is prayer (al-salah), because this word occurs in the Qur'an with the meaning of prayer. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So glorify God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ [al-Rum: 17], and He said: ﴿And glorify your Lord with His praise before the rising of the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130]. What confirms this is that this surah is among the last to be revealed, and "he, peace be upon him, in the last of his illness was saying: the prayer, and what your right hands possess," he was moving it in his chest and his tongue could not grasp it. Then some said: it refers to the prayer of thanks; he prayed eight rak'ahs on the day of the Conquest. Others said: it is the prayer of forenoon (duha). Others said: he prayed eight rak'ahs, four for thanks and four for duha. The naming of prayer as tasbih is because it does not separate from it, and in it is an admonition: that it is obligatory to make your prayer free from kinds of deficiencies in words and deeds. The proponents of the first view argued with the many reports related on this. Aisha narrated: "After the revelation of this surah, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would frequently say: Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You; I seek Your forgiveness and turn to You in repentance." She also said: "The Messenger used to say much in his bowing: Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You, O God, forgive me." And also from her: "The Prophet of God, at the end of his affair, would not stand, nor sit, nor go, nor come, except that he said: Glory be to God and praise be to Him." I said: "O Messenger of God, you say often: Glory be to God and praise be to Him." He said: "I have been commanded with it," and he recited: ﴿When the help of God comes﴾.

And from Ibn Mas'ud: "When this surah was revealed, he, peace be upon him, would frequently say: Glory be to You, O God, and praise be to You, O God, forgive me; indeed You are the Ever-Relenting, the Most Forgiving."
It is related that he said: "Indeed I seek God's forgiveness a hundred times every day."

The third issue: The verse indicates the excellence of glorification and praise, since it was made sufficient in discharging what was obligatory upon him of thanking for the blessing of victory and conquest. Why would it not be so, when His saying "The fast is for Me" is among the greatest virtues of fasting, for He attributed it to His own essence? Then He made the prayer equal to fasting in this honor: ﴿And that the mosques belong to God﴾ [al-Jinn: 18]. This indicates that prayer is far superior to fasting. Then prayer contains remembrances, and for this reason He said: ﴿And the remembrance of God is greater﴾ [al-Ankabut: 45]. And how would it not be so, when praise of Him is known by reason and by revelation to be what He is praised for? As for the manner of prayer, there is no way to it except through the Shari'ah, and for this reason prayer was made like a setting adorned with glorification and magnification.

If it is said: the non-obligation of the glorifications suggests that they are of lower rank than the rest of the actions of prayer, we say: the answer to this is in several aspects:
One of them: The rest of the actions of prayer are things the heart does not incline to, so obligation was needed for them. As for glorification and tahlil, reason calls to it and the spirit is in love with it, so natural love sufficed. For this reason He said: ﴿And those who believe are stronger in love﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165].
The second: His saying "so glorify" is a command, and an unrestricted command is for obligation according to the jurists. And whoever says an unrestricted command is for recommendation says that here it is for obligation by the indication that He joined seeking forgiveness to it, and seeking forgiveness is obligatory, and the right of conjunction is equality between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined.
The third: If they were obligatory, the punishment resulting from abandoning them would be greater, showing greater magnification of them, so He left off obligating them out of fear of this prohibited outcome.

The fourth issue: As for praise (hamd), its explanation has already passed. As for the explanation of His saying: ﴿So glorify your Lord with His praise﴾, they mentioned several aspects:
One of them: The author of the Kashshaf said: that is, say: "Glory be to God and praise be to God," wondering at what He has shown you of His wondrous bounty; that is, combine them, as you say: "I drank the water with the milk" when you combine them by mixing and drinking.
The second: If you praise God, you have glorified Him, because tasbih is included within hamd, since praising Him and thanking Him must necessarily include declaring Him free from deficiencies, for He is not deserving of praise unless He is free from imperfection. For this reason He made the key of the Qur'an the "Praise be to God," and at the conquest of Mecca he said: "Praise be to God who helped His servant," and he did not open his speech with glorification. So His saying: ﴿so glorify with His praise﴾ means: glorify Him through praising Him, that is, glorify Him by this way.

The fourth: It is permissible that its meaning be: glorify, intending that you praise after the glorification, as if he were saying: you cannot combine them verbally, so combine them in intention, just as on the day of sacrifice you intend the prayer, intending to sacrifice after it, so the two rewards gather for you at that time; likewise here.
The fifth: That this "ba'" be the one in your saying: "I did this by the bounty of God," that is, glorify Him with the praise of God and His guidance and His bounty, not with the praise of another. A parallel to this in the hadith of the slander is Aisha's saying: "By the praise of God, not by your praise." The meaning is: glorify Him with His praise, for it is He who guided you apart from others. For this reason it is reported that he, peace be upon him, used to say: "Praise be to God for the praise of God."
The sixth: Al-Suddi related: "with the praise of your Lord," that is, by the command of your Lord.
The seventh: That the "ba'" be an extra connecting particle, and the estimation is: glorify the praise of your Lord. Then there are possibilities:
One of them: choose for Him the purest and most pure praises.
The second: purify the praises of your Lord from showing off and self-display, and from using their mention as a means to worldly corrupt aims.

Third: "Glorify the praises of your Lord" means: keep the praises of your Lord free from saying, "I have brought them" (i.e., that you have achieved praise on your own), as is fitting for Him. This is what He points to in His words: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾ (Surah al-An'am, 91).

Eighth: That is, bring glorification (tasbih) in place of the praise (hamd) that is obligatory upon you. This is because praise is only obligatory in return for blessings, and God's blessings upon us are without limit, so praising Him fully is beyond the capacity of humans. For this reason He said: ﴿And if you tried to count God's blessings, you could not enumerate them﴾ (Surah Ibrahim, 34). It is as if He, exalted is He, is saying: "You are unable to praise Me fully, so bring glorification and declaration of My transcendence in place of praise."

Ninth: In it there is an indication that glorification and praise are two matters, neither of which may be delayed after the other, and it is also inconceivable that they be performed together. Their parallel is one who has both the right of pre-emption (shuf'a, the right to buy a property before others) and the right of return due to a defect. He must say: "I have chosen the pre-emption by returning that sold item." Thus He said: ﴿So glorify with the praise of your Lord﴾, so that both occur together, and he becomes one who praises and glorifies at the same time.

Tenth: The intended meaning may be: "Glorify your heart," that is, purify your heart by contemplating the praise of your Lord. For when you see that everything is from God, you have purified your heart from attention to yourself and your own effort. Thus His words "so glorify" indicate the negation of everything other than God, exalted is He, and His words "with the praise of your Lord" indicate seeing all things as coming from God, exalted is He.

**Fifth issue: Regarding His words "and seek His forgiveness," there are several aspects:**

First: Perhaps he (peace be upon him) used to wish to take revenge on those who harmed him and to ask God to grant him victory. So when he heard ﴿When the help of God comes﴾, he rejoiced. But if this glad tidings had been accompanied by a condition that he not take revenge, that glad tidings would have been spoiled for him. So He mentioned the word "people" and that they would enter the religion of God, and He commanded him to seek forgiveness for those who entered. But it is well known that seeking forgiveness for one who has no sin is not fitting. Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) understood by this route that He, exalted is He, had encouraged him to pardon and to refrain from retaliation. For when He commanded him to seek forgiveness for them, how could it be fitting for him to occupy himself with taking revenge on them? Then He concluded with the word "Oft-Returning" (tawwab), as if saying: accepting repentance is His profession, so whoever asks Him for repentance, He grants it, just as a merchant's profession is selling the goods he has. Whoever asks him for some of those goods, he sells to them, whether the buyer is an enemy or a friend. Likewise, the Lord, glorified is He, accepts repentance whether the penitent is from Mecca or Medina. Then he (peace be upon him) complied with the command of the Lord, exalted is He. When they said to him, "A noble brother and the son of a noble brother," he said to them: ﴿No reproach upon you today; God forgives you﴾ (Surah Yusuf, 92). That is, He commanded me to seek forgiveness for you, so He would not allow me to reject you.

Second: His words "and seek His forgiveness" either mean "seek forgiveness from God for yourself" or "for your community." If the intended meaning is the first, then it depends on whether he committed any disobedience or not. Whoever says that disobedience did proceed from him mentions several reasons for seeking forgiveness:

One: It is not impossible that frequent seeking of forgiveness from him may affect making his sin a minor one.

Two: He was obligated to seek forgiveness so that he would be saved from the sin of persistence.

Three: He was obligated to seek forgiveness so that the seeking of forgiveness would compensate for the minor sin, and so nothing of his reward would be diminished at all.

As for whoever says that no disobedience proceeded from him, he mentions several reasons for this seeking of forgiveness:

One: The seeking of forgiveness by the Prophet is in the manner of glorification, because He described God as "Most Forgiving" (Ghaffar).

Two: God made him worship in this way so that others would follow him, since no accountable person is safe from shortcomings that occur in his worship. In this there is an alert that, despite his great striving and his infallibility, he did not stand in need of seeking forgiveness less; so how about someone other than him?

Three: The seeking of forgiveness was for leaving the more excellent course.

Four: The seeking of forgiveness was because every act of obedience the servant performs, when he compares it with the bounty of the Lord, he finds it falling short of fulfilling the thanks due for that blessing. So let him seek God's forgiveness for that.

Five: The seeking of forgiveness is because of the shortcoming that occurs in the path (suluk). For the traveler to God, when he reaches a station in servanthood and then passes beyond it, after passing beyond it he sees that station as deficient, so he seeks God's forgiveness for it. And since the stages of the journey to God are without limit, the stages of this seeking of forgiveness are necessarily without limit.

As for the second possibility, that the intended meaning is "seek forgiveness for the sin of your community," this is also evident, because He commanded him to seek forgiveness for the sins of his community in His words: ﴿And seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾ (Surah Muhammad, 19). Here, since the community is large, that seeking of forgiveness becomes more binding and more important. Likewise, if we say the intended meaning here is that he seek forgiveness for himself and for his community.

* * *

**Sixth issue: There is a problem in the verse. Repentance precedes all acts of obedience, then praise precedes glorification, because praise is caused by bestowal, and bestowal may proceed from the one who is transcendent and from others. So it should have been that the beginning is with seeking forgiveness, then after it he mentions praise, then after it he mentions glorification. So what is the reason that it was mentioned in reverse of this order?**

Its answer is in several aspects:

First: Perhaps He began with the most noble, then the more noble descending to the less noble, then the less noble, as an alert that descent from the Creator to the creation is nobler than ascent from the creation to the Creator.

Second: In it there is an alert that glorification and praise that proceed from the servant, when they are set against the majesty and might of God, become themselves a sin, and so seeking forgiveness from them becomes obligatory.

Third: Glorification and praise are an indication of exalting the command of God, while seeking forgiveness is an indication of compassion toward the creation of [God]. The first is like prayer (salah), and the second is like almsgiving (zakah). Just as prayer precedes almsgiving, so it is here.

* * *

**Seventh issue: The verse indicates that it was obligatory for him (peace and blessings be upon him) to proclaim the glorification and the seeking of forgiveness, and this is from several aspects:**

One: He (peace and blessings be upon him) was commanded to convey the surah to the whole community, so that the transmission of the Qur'an remains mutawatir (transmitted by so many chains that its authenticity is certain), and so that we know that he performed the duty of conveying revelation well. Therefore it was obligatory for him to perform glorification and seeking of forgiveness openly, so that this purpose would be achieved.

Two: It is among the aims that the Messenger become an example for the community, so that they do at times of blessing and at times of trial what the Messenger did: renewing thanks and praise when a blessing is renewed.

Three: In what is witnessed, the most common practice is that a person begins with praise at the start of a matter. So God commanded His Messenger to praise and seek forgiveness constantly, at every time and moment, so that a distinction would arise between him and others. Then He said, "and seek His forgiveness," at the time when his soul was announced to him, so that the community would do the same at the approach of their terms.

* * *

**Eighth issue: There are questions regarding the verse:**

One: He said ﹛Oft-Returning﹜ in the past tense (kana), while our need is for His acceptance in the future.

Two: Why did He not say "Forgiving" (Ghaffar), as He said in the Surah of Nuh?

Three: He said "the help of God" and said "in the religion of God," so why did He not say "with the praise of God," but rather said "with the praise of your Lord"?

The answer to the first question has several aspects:

One: This is more eloquent, as if He is saying: Did I not praise you by saying that you are "the best community brought forth for mankind" (Surah Al 'Imran, 110)? Then those who came before you: I would accept their repentance, like the Jews. For after the manifestation of great miracles, the splitting of the sea, the lifting of the mountain, and the descent of manna and quail, they disobeyed their Lord and committed abominations. When they repented, I accepted their repentance. So if I accepted repentance from those before you, should I not accept it from you?

Two: Long ago I began accepting the repentance of sinners, and commencing something creates a obligation to continue it, so how much more so in the generosity of the Most Merciful?

Three: I was Oft-Returning before I commanded you to seek forgiveness. Should I not accept, now that I have commanded you to seek forgiveness?

Four: It may be an indication of lightening their offense, meaning: you are not the first to sin and repent; rather it is my practice, and an offense is a calamity for the one who commits it, and a calamity, when it becomes general, becomes lighter.

Five: It is as if it corresponds to what is said:
"God has done well in what has passed; so He will do well in what remains."

The answer to the second question has several aspects:

One: Perhaps He specified this community with an added nobility, because it is not said of the attributes of a servant that he is "Forgiving" (Ghaffar), but it is said that he is "Oft-Returning" (tawwab) when he is one who performs repentance. So God, exalted is He, says: "You were my namesake from the beginning of the matter: you are a believer and I am a believer, though the meaning differs. So repent until you become my namesake at the end of the matter: you are Oft-Returning and I am Oft-Returning." Furthermore, the sense of "Oft-Returning" with regard to God is that He accepts repentance abundantly, so He alerted that it is obligatory upon the servant that his performing repentance be abundant.

Two: It was only said "Oft-Returning" because the speaker may say, "I seek God's forgiveness," while not being a penitent. From this is His words (peace be upon him): "The one who seeks forgiveness with his tongue while persisting in his heart is like one who mocks his Lord." If it is said: one may say, "I repent," without being penitent. We say: then he would be lying, because repentance is the name for returning and regret, unlike seeking forgiveness, for in it one is not lying. So the sense of the speech becomes: "seek forgiveness from Him by way of repentance." In this there is an alert that the ends of deeds must be with repentance and seeking forgiveness, and likewise the ends of deeds. And it is narrated that he did not sit in any gathering without concluding it with seeking forgiveness.

The answer to the third question: God, exalted is He, observed justice. So He mentioned the name of the Essence twice and the name of the Act twice: one is "the Lord," and the second is "the Oft-Returning." Since nurturing (tarbiyah) occurs first and the quality of accepting repentance occurs last, He therefore mentioned the name "the Lord" first and the name "the Oft-Returning" last.

* * *

**Ninth issue: The Companions agreed that this surah indicated that it was an announcement of the death of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is narrated that al-'Abbas understood this and wept, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "What makes you weep?" He said, "Your soul has been announced to you." He said, "The matter is as you say." It is also said that Ibn 'Abbas was the one who said that, and the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "This youth has been given much knowledge."**

It is narrated that 'Umar used to honor Ibn 'Abbas, bring him close, and permit him to attend with the people of Badr. 'Abd al-Rahman said: "Will you permit this youth to attend with us, when among our sons there is one like him?" 'Umar said: "Because he is one of whom you know." Ibn 'Abbas said: "So he permitted them one day, and permitted me to attend with them. He asked them about the words of God: ﴿When the help of God comes﴾, and it is as if he only asked them for my sake. Some of them said: 'God commanded His Prophet that when he conquers, he should seek His forgiveness and turn to Him.' I said: 'It is not so; rather, his soul was announced to him.' Then 'Umar said: 'I know nothing of it except what you know.' Then he said: 'How do you blame me for it after what you have seen?'"

It is also narrated that when this surah was revealed, he delivered a sermon and said: "Indeed, a servant was given the choice by God between this world and meeting Him and the Hereafter, and he chose meeting God." The questioner said: "How does this surah indicate this meaning?"

The answer has several aspects:

One: Some of them said: They knew that only because of what we have related, that the Messenger delivered a sermon right after the surah and mentioned the choice.

Two: When He mentioned the attainment of victory and the conquest and the entry of people into the religion in multitudes, this indicated the attainment of perfection and completion, and that is followed by decline, as it is said:
"When a thing reaches completion, its decline draws near;
expect its decline when it is said, 'It has become complete.'"

Third: He commanded him to glorify (tasbih), praise (hamd) and seek forgiveness (istighfar) without restriction, and his being occupied with that would prevent him from being occupied with the affairs of the community (ummah). So this was like an alert that the matter of conveying (tabligh) had been completed and perfected, and that necessarily entails death, because if he remained after that he would be like one dismissed from the prophetic mission (risalah), and that is not permissible.

Fourth: His saying, ﴿and seek His forgiveness﴾, is an alert to the nearness of the appointed term (ajal). It is as if He were saying: the time has drawn near and the departure has approached, so prepare for the matter. And by it He alerted him that the way of the intelligent person, when his term draws near, is to increase in repentance (tawbah).

Fifth: It is as if it were said to him: the final goal of your seeking in this world was this which you have attained, namely victory (nasr), conquest (fath) and dominion (istila'). And Allah the Exalted promised you by His saying: ﴿And the Hereafter is better for you than the first [life]﴾. So when you have found the utmost of your aims in this world, then move on to the Hereafter, so that you may attain those lofty felicities.

The tenth issue: We have mentioned that the more correct view is that the surah was revealed before the conquest of Mecca (Fath Makkah). As for those who said that it was revealed after the conquest of Mecca, al-Mawardi mentioned that he (peace be upon him) did not remain after the revelation of this surah except sixty days, constantly glorifying and seeking forgiveness. Muqatil said: he lived after it for a year, and when ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3] was revealed, he lived after it eighty days; then the verse of al-Kalalah was revealed, and he lived after it fifty days; then ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128] was revealed, and he lived after it thirty-five days; then ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281] was revealed, and he lived after it eleven days. In another narration, he lived after it seven days. And Allah knows best how that was.
